summary.text: Charles's law says that when the pressure on a sample of dry gas is held constant, its volume is in direct proportion to its Kelvin temperature.
So as the absolute temperature goes up, the volume of the gas goes up in proportion.
It is named after Jacques Charles, who worked on it in the 1780s, though without a firm record the law cannot be attributed to him.

facts.label: Dalton's finding
facts.value: All gases and vapours he studied expanded by the same amount

facts.label: Earlier ideas
facts.value: Amontons and Hauksbee described the basic principles a century before

items.prompt: A sealed, flexible bag of dry gas is carried from a cool room into a warm one, with the pressure on it unchanged. What happens to its volume?

options.label: It increases in proportion to the temperature
It decreases as the gas warms
It stays the same size
It increases only at the moment of the move

items.explain: At constant pressure, volume and Kelvin temperature are in direct proportion, so warming increases volume.

items.prompt: The Kelvin temperature of a gas doubles while the pressure on it stays constant. What happens to its volume?

options.label: It halves
It stays the same
It doubles
It quadruples

items.explain: Volume is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature at constant pressure.

items.prompt: Why do historians hesitate to give Jacques Charles the credit for the law?

options.label: He published it after Gay-Lussac did
He used a pressure that kept changing
He worked only with vapours, never gases
His work was unpublished and no firm record of it exists

items.explain: Charles's work from the 1780s was unpublished, and in the absence of a firm record the law cannot be attributed to him.

items.prompt: Dalton tested many gases and vapours between two fixed temperatures. What did he find?

options.label: Lighter gases expanded much more
All of them expanded by the same amount
Vapours expanded but gases did not
Each gas expanded by a different amount

items.explain: Dalton demonstrated that all the gases and vapours he studied expanded by the same amount between two fixed points of temperature.

items.prompt: A gas is heated while the pressure on it is also changing. Why can Charles's law alone not give its volume?

options.label: The law applies only to liquids that are heated
The law ignores temperature altogether
The law applies only when the pressure on the sample is constant
The law applies only to gases at 0 °C

items.explain: The volume-temperature proportion holds when the pressure on a dry gas sample is held constant.

items.prompt: How did Dalton's measurements go further than Gay-Lussac's?

options.label: He tested one gas where Gay-Lussac tested many
He measured only at the fixed points of water
He used Kelvin thermometers instead of mercury ones
He also measured the volume at two intermediate temperatures

items.explain: Dalton measured not only at the fixed points of water but also at two intermediate points.
